title: Orders evidence leaks across tenants before ranking
context: An internal modernization assistant serves 40 tenants. Global top-3 retrieval returns beta tenant orders notes for an authenticated alpha engineer. Corpus contains two revisions of orders.md, an overlapping duplicate chunk and an admin-only note. Retrieval must finish within a 150 ms teaching target and preserve source/version/chunk provenance; security failure is unacceptable even if Recall@3 improves.
requirements: Resolve tenant and role from verified middleware session independently of requested tenant.
Filter authorized corpus before any scoring, deduplication or top-k selection.
Choose newest authorized source revision and collapse overlapping identical content.
Return citations containing tenant, source, version and chunk; cap k at five.

questions.prompt: Where does tenant authorization belong, and why is post-filtering global top-k insufficient?
questions.answer: Start with the verified principal established by authentication middleware, then compare the requested tenant with that principal's allowed scope. The request body and model-generated tool arguments never establish identity. Filter the candidate corpus by tenant and document role before scoring; then choose current revisions and deduplicate within that scope. Global top-k followed by filtering is insufficient because unauthorized text or metadata can enter intermediate components, logs and rerankers, and unauthorized high-scoring documents can crowd out valid results. Recheck authorization when fetching the final document and assembling context because permissions can change after index lookup. In this fixture the beta private note and alpha admin-only note must never appear among scored sources. Record denied requests separately from genuine no-evidence abstention, without disclosing private document existence.
checks: Verified session independent of request tenant
Fetch/context recheck and no existence leak

questions.prompt: How should overlapping chunks and multiple revisions affect citations and relevance scores?
questions.answer: Preserve source identity, revision and chunk offsets during ingestion. Select the newest allowed published revision for each source, rather than allowing old and new runtime facts to compete as independent evidence. Identical overlapping chunks from that revision should count once for ranking and context, while their provenance remains recoverable. Deduplicate using source, revision and normalized content or a content hash; do not collapse different tenants or contradictory independent sources merely because words overlap. The reference picks one deterministic chunk identifier for identical content and returns orders.md version 2. A citation must identify the actual chosen bytes or manifest hash so later review can reproduce evidence. Recall should be evaluated using declared document or passage units; duplicated chunks must not inflate the numerator. Report unresolved conflicting sources instead of deciding that more repeated text means stronger truth.
checks: Duplicate evidence does not inflate score

hints: Begin by listing which fixture documents alpha engineer can access, before calculating any overlap score.
Build current-version map only from eligible documents; use source plus revision plus text for deduplication.
Track scored source IDs in test-only output; assert beta/private and admin documents never enter ranking.
acceptance: orders query returns exactly alpha:orders.md@v2#c1; duplicate c2 omitted.
Alpha requesting beta and unknown session each raises PermissionError before ranking.
Viewer receives no engineer-only hits; unknown query returns empty hits.
All returned hits carry current source version and deterministic citation.
pitfalls: Filtering only after top-k loses allowed evidence and exposes unauthorized intermediate data.
Using tenant supplied by model as trusted identity permits cross-tenant access.
twist: Roles are revoked while a response is waiting for reranking. Explain final fetch reauthorization and cache invalidation.
solution: Implement identity and authorization before relevance. The first reference lookup obtains a fixture principal from a server-owned session map. A requested beta tenant under the alpha session is rejected immediately. Eligible chunks then undergo current-source selection, producing orders revision 2 rather than obsolete revision 1. Sorting by source and chunk makes duplicate selection reproducible; the identical overlapping chunk is removed before lexical overlap ranking. Ranking sees neither the beta private note nor the alpha admin-only note. The successful response therefore contains one current orders citation, not three repeated or unauthorized passages. Negative fixtures cover forged session, mismatched tenant, viewer role and missing lexical evidence. Discuss how a production implementation replaces fixture session data with verified authentication and adds authorization epoch checks at final fetch. The bundled overlap scorer intentionally teaches control placement without installing embeddings; it makes no semantic-quality or 150 ms production claim. Time the local code separately if you want performance evidence.

assignment.objective: Build authorization-first retrieval with current unique citations.
steps: Write immutable principal and versioned chunk records.
Implement tenant/role filtering before score computation.
Add current-source selection and deterministic duplicate collapse.
Run reference self-tests, then inject a high-scoring unauthorized note and prove it never ranks.

title: Yesterday’s cache survives today’s deletion and poison quarantine
context: Every hour 2,000 modernization notes change. A runtime source moves from Java 8 to 17; a dependency README contains secret-upload instructions; an approved note is deleted. Existing cache entries still cite old facts. Index freshness target is five minutes and revoked access must stop immediately, independently of the ingestion backlog.
requirements: Version every source and reject stale or duplicate version updates.
Track index epoch and authorization epoch in cache keys.
Keep quarantined and tombstoned sources out of retrieval.
Revalidate fetched citation against current trusted source manifest.

questions.prompt: How do you prevent an old cached answer from surviving source deletion or access revocation?
questions.answer: Maintain a trusted manifest that records the current source revision, publication status and content hash. Deletion changes that manifest and advances an index epoch; it is not merely removal from one vector shard. Cache identity includes the principal's authorization context, authorization epoch and index snapshot version. Final fetch checks each cited source against the current manifest, so a stale cache key cannot authorize deleted evidence. Revocation should deny at the authorization boundary immediately even if asynchronous document deletion has not finished. Use tombstones to prevent late ingestion messages from resurrecting old versions. Track ingestion lag separately from access enforcement latency. In the reference, publication of revision 3 as deleted leaves zero live runtime hits and a query explicitly pinned to the prior snapshot raises an error. Explain how caches, indexes and in-flight context assembly all consume these epochs.

questions.prompt: What should happen to a README containing instructions to upload secrets?
questions.answer: Treat retrieved text as untrusted evidence, regardless of whether its repository is otherwise approved. This exercise places the known poisoned fixture in a quarantined publication state maintained by a trusted ingestion/review path; the text never grants tool authority. A keyword detector alone cannot reliably identify every indirect injection, so do not claim the quarantine logic makes arbitrary documents safe. Preserve provenance and route suspicious instructions to review while retaining normal facts only through an approved parsing or publication decision. Tool execution must still independently deny secret reads and unauthorized egress. Evaluate both explicit malicious examples and benign instructions so false-positive rates remain visible. Record whether the source was quarantined, rejected or partly extracted and avoid logging secret-bearing raw text. Replaying an older approved version must not clear quarantine or defeat a newer tombstone.

hints: Make source revision monotonic; stale events must fail before modifying live state.
Include both ACL and index epochs in cache key, rather than clearing one process-local dictionary and hoping.
Publish revision 3 tombstone after revision 2, then query old epoch and current epoch separately.
acceptance: Revision 1 Java 8 is replaced by revision 2 Java 17.
Quarantined poisoned note never enters live hits.
Deleted revision 3 yields zero runtime hits and cannot be resurrected by revision 2.
Old snapshot query and revoked principal are rejected; cache epoch changes visible.
pitfalls: Index deletion alone does not remove cached or in-flight evidence.
A detector catching one poison phrase is not general injection prevention.
twist: One index shard is offline during deletion. Define fail-closed evidence policy and a maximum stale-read contract.
solution: Separate three processes: trusted source state, derived index publication and query access. The manifest advances monotonically whenever an approved revision, quarantine decision or deletion is recorded. The reference advances an index epoch and gives cache entries a distinct identity for each corpus state. Current-query selection excludes quarantine and deletion before result assembly, while explicit old-snapshot requests are rejected. Authorization revocation advances its own epoch and the fixture rejects the revoked principal; production middleware would obtain that principal state from current identity policy. Self-tests replay an obsolete version, attempt an old snapshot and confirm that deleted runtime content disappears while known poison remains excluded. The architecture exercise then adds durable outbox events, atomic index swaps, idempotent consumers and tombstones retained longer than maximum message delay. Distinguish five-minute content freshness from immediate access revocation. The code simulates one source namespace and does not offer multi-shard consistency or a general malicious-document classifier.

assignment.objective: Implement version-monotonic publication and cache invalidation with quarantine/deletion.
steps: Define source manifest with version, review state and hash.
Advance corpus/auth epochs and include them in cache identity.
Reject stale versions and explicit stale snapshots.
Test replacement, quarantine, tombstone, late update and revoked principal fixtures.

title: Schema-valid answer invents a target framework
context: An assistant answers 300 runtime questions daily. Evidence says orders currently uses Java 17, but a generated plan adds “Spring 6 upgrade completed” with a real-looking citation. Reviewers allow at most 1% unsupported critical claims and need explicit abstention when target-framework facts are absent.
requirements: Separate source citation existence from claim entailment.
Validate claim field, exact value/type, tenant and current revision.
Return explicit abstention for missing or conflicting authorized facts.
Keep source parsing and output checking deterministic for the fixture.

questions.prompt: Why is a real citation insufficient to validate a recommendation?
questions.answer: A citation proves that a source can be referenced; it does not prove that every adjacent claim is present in that source. Validate the cited revision is current, authorized and actually supports the specific field and value. In the fixture runtime_major 17 is an extracted trusted fact, while target_framework and deployment_succeeded are absent. A response that cites the runtime source but invents framework completion must fail semantic validation even if its JSON shape is valid. Also enforce exact types because Python treats True as equal to 1 in ordinary comparisons. For free-form narratives, structured evidence checks cover only the declared claims; additional human or independently calibrated assessment may be needed. Keep recommendation status as a proposal unless execution receipts establish actual outcomes. Do not repair unsupported claims merely by lowering temperature, because authority and evidence validity remain application responsibilities.

questions.prompt: When should the assistant abstain, and how do you evaluate that behavior?
questions.answer: Abstain when no authorized current evidence supports the requested field, when equally trusted sources conflict, or when required context was excluded by budget or freshness policy. An abstention should state the missing evidence category and safe next retrieval action without revealing hidden tenant facts. In this fixture the unknown target_framework field produces no claims and an explicit missing-or-conflicting-evidence reason. Evaluate supported extraction and no-answer cases separately: count correct factual answers, unsupported claims, correct abstentions and unnecessary abstentions with clear denominators. A system that always abstains may be safe on one metric but useless overall, so pair critical unsupported-rate limits with answer coverage and task-success requirements. Freeze those thresholds before comparing configurations. The deterministic reference tests missing fields, fake citations, stale revisions, other tenants and wrong types; it does not grade arbitrary prose or demonstrate a one-percent production rate.
checks: Coverage and unsupported rate jointly measured

hints: Start from a structured source fact, not a generated sentence.
Require current tenant-matching citation, then check the particular field/value with strict type equality.
Test a cited-but-unsupported deployment claim; valid citation must not make it pass.
acceptance: Current runtime answer returns 17 with alpha:orders@v2#runtime citation.
Unknown framework request abstains with zero claims.
Fake, stale and beta citations rejected.
Wrong field/value and Boolean-for-integer substitutions rejected; cross-tenant request denied.
pitfalls: Checking only citation ID allows claims unsupported by the cited text.
An always-abstaining system can hide poor utility behind low unsupported rate.
twist: Two authorized current files disagree on runtime version. Require a conflict answer rather than majority voting repeated chunks.
solution: Use a reviewed source snapshot whose structured facts are extracted independently of response generation. The answer function first resolves the verified session and rejects tenant mismatch. It searches only current authorized sources containing the requested field. Exactly one supported fact allows an extraction response; zero or multiple candidate facts produce abstention, keeping uncertainty explicit. The validator then independently checks output shape, known citation, tenant, current status and exact field/value/type. Negative fixtures show that real source identity does not authorize a fake deployment outcome, an obsolete source cannot establish current runtime, and Boolean values cannot impersonate integer facts. Report these as nine local contract fixtures rather than natural-language groundedness performance. Extend the exercise by attaching parser provenance and supporting quotes, by distinguishing consistent duplicate sources from true conflicts, and by creating a reviewed no-answer evaluation set. Any future model remains outside the trust decision: it may draft claims, but trusted evidence validation decides which structured claims can be emitted.

assignment.objective: Write claim-level validation and missing-evidence abstention without a model.
steps: Define trusted current/stale source facts and verified principal lookup.
Implement answer extraction with explicit no-evidence/conflict abstention.
Validate each structured claim independently of answer builder.
Run nine fixtures and add a genuine conflicting-current-source test.

title: Exact Java symbols vanish in a dense-only search redesign
context: A modernization team searches 80,000 source chunks. Queries include exact com.acme.LegacyClient symbols and conceptual phrases such as “retry duplicates payment.” Dense-only retrieval improves paraphrase demos but misses exact versions. Retrieval budget is 120 ms before reranking, context allows 2,400 tokens, and each tenant requires an isolated authorized candidate set.
requirements: Compare lexical, dense and hybrid retrieval on the same labeled queries.
Preserve exact symbols/version tokens while selecting an embedding model locally.
Use explicit rank fusion and spend rerank budget on bounded candidates.
Evaluate query-family slices and context evidence coverage, not only aggregate hit rate.

questions.prompt: How would you design hybrid retrieval without hiding failures behind a single similarity score?
questions.answer: Maintain independent lexical and dense candidate lists after tenant and document authorization. Lexical indexing preserves exact identifiers, package coordinates and runtime versions; dense representations address paraphrases and conceptual similarity. Fuse ranked lists using a declared method such as reciprocal rank fusion rather than summing incompatible raw scores without calibration. Deduplicate by source revision and evidence unit before context selection. Bound each retriever's candidate count and give reranking an explicit deadline and fallback policy. Evaluate exact-symbol, version-sensitive and conceptual query slices against labeled relevant passages on the same frozen corpus. The offline references provide lexical controls only, so a dense extension requires installed local model weights and a real vector index; random vectors cannot stand in for measured semantic quality. Prefer the simplest configuration meeting slice recall, authorization and latency requirements instead of adding every retrieval feature by default.
checks: Real local embeddings and per-family evaluation

questions.prompt: How do you allocate 2,400 context tokens after retrieval returns twenty relevant chunks?
questions.answer: Reserve prompt instructions, question and response allowance according to the selected model's actual tokenizer contract, then allocate the remaining evidence budget. Prefer evidence directly answering the question, preserve complete definitions or contract boundaries where possible, and remove overlapping duplicates. Include compact citations for every retained source revision. Do not cut a Java signature from its error-handling logic merely to satisfy a fixed character window; symbol-aware chunks or a focused follow-up lookup may be more useful. Mark excluded evidence and truncation visibly so a downstream answer cannot silently imply complete repository coverage. Measure evidence coverage at the same declared passage or fact unit used by labels and pair it with answer usefulness. If mandatory supporting material exceeds the budget, ask a narrower question or abstain on the unproven part. Token cost, rerank latency and recall changes should be reported together for this exact query cohort.
checks: Visible omitted evidence and narrowed answer

hints: Create three query cohorts: exact symbol, exact version and paraphrase; label before tuning.
Try rank fusion on lists rather than direct addition of unrelated score scales.
Write a context manifest listing retained, duplicate and excluded chunks with budget reasons.
acceptance: Design reports Recall@5 and MRR@5 for each query family with sample count.
Every retriever/reranker consumes only authorized current evidence.
Context manifest shows at most 2,400 selected evidence tokens under stated tokenizer.
Deadline fallback and no-local-embedding limitation documented.
pitfalls: A good paraphrase demo cannot establish exact-identifier recall.
Characters divided by four is not a universal token count.
twist: Dense model weights are unavailable offline. Deliver honest lexical baseline and optional integration contract rather than fake embeddings.
solution: Start with frozen query labels and source revisions so retrieval choices can be compared fairly. Build an exact lexical baseline first and identify its conceptual misses. A locally installed dense retriever becomes a second candidate generator; it never receives documents excluded by ACL. Fuse ranks using a pinned formula, deduplicate repeated source evidence and send only a small authorized pool to a reranker. Record deadline behavior explicitly: if reranking fails, use the permitted fused order and mark that fallback, rather than silently returning global candidates. Assemble evidence within the tokenizer-based budget while retaining source IDs, version hashes and omitted-evidence reasons. Compare all configurations on exact symbols, versions and paraphrases separately, including negative/no-answer cases. A useful principal defense explains which failure was fixed, what latency/cost was added and why remaining misses matter. This scenario is design-only: no embeddings, hybrid search or semantic-quality results are fabricated by the static tutorial, and all service targets remain requirements rather than observed measurements.

title: Code-aware chunks break a serialization explanation
context: A Java migration assistant chunks every 500 characters with 100-character overlap. A method signature and its custom serializer fall into separate chunks; generated answers claim parity despite changed null handling. There are 12,000 Java files, generated code may be excluded, and context budget is 1,800 tokens per question.
requirements: Use symbol/build-aware boundaries where available and mark unresolved reflection/generated edges.
Attach file revision, line span and containing symbol to chunks.
Create relevant-evidence labels for null, encoding and serialization cases.
Compare fixed-window and structure-aware chunking without changing generation configuration.

questions.prompt: What should chunking preserve for a code-modernization question?
questions.answer: Preserve evidence needed to reason about behavior, including method signature, relevant body, serialization configuration and caller contract when available. Symbol-aware parsing gives useful boundaries but may still miss reflection, generated adapters or runtime registrations, so chunk metadata should state those coverage limits. Keep file revision, line span and symbol identity with each passage; a chunk without provenance cannot support a reproducible migration claim. Use focused neighbor or dependency lookup when a behavior crosses symbols rather than inflating every chunk indiscriminately. Label concrete questions about null handling, encoding and payload compatibility before selecting overlap sizes. Compare retrieval and context coverage under a fixed token budget so larger chunks do not receive an unfair advantage. Passing a chunking experiment improves available evidence, but it does not prove behavior parity; actual contract tests on the approved Java artifact remain required before release.

questions.prompt: How do you measure whether structure-aware chunks improved this failure?
questions.answer: Freeze repository revisions and a question set whose relevant units identify the serializer, caller and configuration needed for each answer. Run both chunking strategies through the same retrieval, ranking and context policy. Count whether every required evidence unit appears in the selected context, not merely whether any passage shares the word serializer. Record token consumption and duplication because large chunks can improve apparent recall while exhausting context and hurting other evidence. Separately assess the answer's claim correctness and cite validity using expected facts or reviewed judgments. For null-handling parity, run behavior tests on before and after binaries once a patch exists; a plausible narrative is not execution evidence. Report per-question regressions and generated/reflection cases as unassessed if parser coverage is absent. Select a change only when its measured evidence coverage and operational costs meet the preregistered threshold.
checks: Required evidence coverage and token costs

hints: Label the serializer, caller and config as three distinct required evidence units.
Compare equal token budgets, not equal chunk counts.
Explain which dynamic edges a Java parser cannot resolve and what runtime evidence fills them.
acceptance: Design includes symbol, revision and line-span chunk metadata.
Experiment pairs both chunk strategies on identical question IDs.
Null/encoding/serialization questions have explicit evidence labels.
Coverage report distinguishes retrieval success, answer correctness and executed parity.
pitfalls: Bigger chunks can improve recall while reducing useful context diversity.
AST availability does not prove complete runtime dependency coverage.
twist: Serializer is loaded by reflection from config. Describe evidence fallback and uncertainty annotation.
solution: Reproduce the failure with one Java fixture question before changing global chunk settings. Identify the missing evidence: serializer implementation, caller expectations and runtime configuration. Define structure-aware boundaries around those units and add compact file/symbol provenance rather than taking arbitrary windows. Build an experiment where both old and new chunkers receive the same repository revision, question labels and 1,800-token evidence limit. Measure whether all required units survive retrieval and assembly, then review the resulting explanation for unsupported parity claims. Keep dynamic wiring and generated code as explicit coverage gaps; request build/runtime configuration or contract receipts where static parsing cannot answer. If a transformation is proposed, baseline and post-change tests must verify null and payload behavior separately from retrieval quality. The final decision record states which code families improved, which questions regressed, the added parse/index cost and the unresolved cases. This is a design/debug exercise with no claimed AST implementation or production parity result.

title: Repository versions conflict during a release incident
context: At 09:00 production runs release hash A while branch head advances to B. RAG index mixes docs from A, B and an unapproved draft. An incident commander asks whether a runtime dependency can be removed in the next 30 minutes. There are 500 services, no complete dynamic call graph and a 99.9% retrieval availability goal.
requirements: Bind each question to environment/deployed revision independently of branch head.
Separate approved release evidence, draft plans and unknown runtime edges.
Require conflict/coverage reporting before dependency-removal recommendations.
Design incident fallback when current evidence is unavailable.

questions.prompt: Which repository revision should a production incident answer use?
questions.answer: Resolve the deployed artifact and environment from trusted release metadata before selecting code evidence. Branch head is not necessarily production, and the latest document may describe an unapproved future change. Filter or route evidence by the exact release hash, tenant and deployment target relevant to the incident. Show when a source is release-bound, draft or stale; do not merge contradictory runtime facts into a confident answer. For removing a dependency, include static callers, build metadata, configuration and runtime evidence, and state dynamic/reflection gaps. An empty graph neighborhood cannot establish that a library is unused. If production revision A evidence is missing, return a scoped uncertainty statement and request artifact/config receipts rather than answering from branch B. Availability goals cannot justify giving a high-confidence unsafe recommendation; an evidence-unavailable response may still be a valid service response under the declared contract.
checks: Deployed revision from trusted release state

questions.prompt: How do you preserve availability when exact-release evidence is temporarily unavailable?
questions.answer: Separate service availability from evidence completeness and decision authority. The endpoint can remain available while returning an explicit evidence-unavailable or partial-analysis result for release A. Provide approved immutable release metadata and a safe next diagnostic action, but avoid substituting newer branch facts without labeling the mismatch. Cache exact-release evidence by immutable revision and current authorization context, retaining prior approved manifests for incident replay. Prioritize indexing the affected service and use build/runtime receipts to fill declared graph gaps. A degraded response should enumerate what is known, what is stale and what action is blocked. Dependency removal stays human-controlled and gated by reviewed parity tests on the intended release candidate. Define an SLO for correct evidence-bound responses as well as latency, because a fast invented answer is operationally worse than an honest abstention during an incident.
checks: Immutable revision cache plus live auth
Removal action stays gated by evidence

hints: Name production hash A, branch hash B and draft status before drawing dependency conclusions.
List evidence required to prove a removal is safe, including runtime wiring.
Define an incident response that stays useful while refusing unsupported removal approval.
acceptance: Answer provenance identifies exact environment and deployed revision.
Draft/B evidence never silently presented as production A.
Dependency-removal decision records graph gaps and missing parity tests.
Degraded/abstention response and recovery/indexing priority specified.
pitfalls: Latest revision is not necessarily deployed revision.
Retrieval availability cannot certify action safety.
twist: A hotfix changes config without source revision. Include config/deployment manifest identity in evidence binding.
solution: Treat incident retrieval as a versioned operational evidence system. Begin by obtaining production artifact A and its configuration/deployment manifest IDs from trusted release state. Query only approved sources compatible with that tuple and keep branch B or drafts in separate, clearly labeled comparison context. Summarize build/static evidence and enumerate unresolved runtime links such as reflection, plugin loading or generated service registration. For the requested dependency removal, require a reviewed plan and tests covering affected contracts; the RAG answer cannot authorize the change. If exact-release evidence is unavailable, return a structured degraded result with known facts, stale sources and missing diagnostics, preserving access checks and immutable citation identity. Recover by prioritizing ingestion of relevant release artifacts rather than reindexing all 500 services blindly. Discuss the distinction between 99.9% endpoint availability and correct evidence availability. No completed removal, incident recovery or dependency graph is asserted by this design-only scenario; the learner must attach actual artifacts before claiming those outcomes.

title: Approved Java diff is replaced before the test receipt arrives
context: A modernization worker proposes a 12-line Java patch. Human approves output hash H, but model later changes two lines and submits matching attacker-chosen approval/artifact fields. A test receipt is validly signed yet belongs to another artifact. No production deployment is allowed in the lab; only exact-artifact eligibility may be reported.
requirements: Register reviewed output hash in trusted policy outside requester fields.
Bind input revision, scoped path and approved output bytes before applying.
Require trusted issuer, successful gate status, exact artifact and gate identity in receipts.
Recheck actual file hash after gate and before release-review eligibility.

questions.prompt: Why do equal approval_hash and artifact_hash fields fail to establish real approval?
questions.answer: Both fields can be controlled by the caller or generated by a model, so equality proves only internal consistency of an untrusted request. Approval must be registered through a trusted human-review channel that records the reviewed artifact, input revision, scope and target. When applying a patch, compare both the claimed approval and hash of proposed bytes against that trusted record. Check the source file still matches the approved input revision and enforce the allowlisted path before writing. A new diff or changed bytes invalidates prior approval even if the requester supplies a newly matching pair of hashes. In the reference, Authority is constructed from fixture review state separately from the request. The malicious matching-hash case must fail without modifying the file. Keep patch approval and deployment approval distinct; local test eligibility is not permission to deploy.

questions.prompt: Can a signed successful receipt be accepted without checking its artifact and gate?
questions.answer: A signature establishes integrity and signer provenance for the receipt, not that it describes the artifact now under consideration. Validate the issuer is a trusted executor, status is executed successfully, artifact hash equals the reviewed output and gate identity matches the required behavior test. Then compare the actual file or immutable bundle hash to that output again, because a post-test edit can make a formerly correct receipt stale. A signed failed receipt, different-artifact receipt or unrelated gate must block eligibility rather than being counted as proof that something ran. Protect the signing key outside model/tool proposal authority and include run/input identities in production receipts. The reference uses a fixture-only HMAC key and simulated gate data, so its passing result proves validation logic, not that Java contracts or deployment actually occurred.
checks: Fixture receipts not fabricated execution claim

hints: Write trusted review record first; do not create it from request approval_hash.
Hash proposed bytes and current input separately; compare both against review record.
Sign a deliberately failed receipt with real fixture key and prove validation still rejects it.
acceptance: Approved exact bytes apply once source hash matches.
Equal attacker-selected hashes, changed scope and wrong tenant fail before write.
Signed failed/wrong-artifact/wrong-gate/wrong-issuer receipts rejected.
Post-gate file edit blocks eligibility; result explicitly says deployed=false.
pitfalls: A signature without status/artifact checks accepts authentic but irrelevant evidence.
Approval created automatically from proposed bytes is not a human approval boundary.
twist: Build creates generated files outside reviewed diff. Bind release approval to complete deployable artifact, not source patch alone.
solution: Create a review record from a trusted fixture setup that knows expected input and reviewed output bytes. Keep this record separate from model-proposed request fields. Patch application checks verified principal, tenant, exact file scope, current input hash and proposed output hash before writing. A request with equal attacker-generated hashes fails because neither matches the registered reviewed output. Release-review eligibility then requires a correctly signed receipt with trusted issuer, successful status, exact artifact and named gate. Recompute actual file hash at that point to catch edits after testing. The self-tests deliberately sign failed, wrong-artifact and wrong-gate receipts, demonstrating that authenticity alone is insufficient. Explain how a production worker would replace the fixture key with isolated executor signing, add immutable build artifacts and bind environment/target identity to approval. This example performs only a tiny local byte patch and receipt checks; it does not run Java tests or deploy. The operational decision must remain eligible-for-review rather than falsely reporting completed modernization.

assignment.objective: Enforce independently registered exact-artifact approval and receipt binding.
steps: Create trusted review state from original and reviewed fixture bytes.
Implement path/input/output/tenant checks before writing.
Validate signed receipt status, issuer, required gate and artifact.
Execute matching-attacker-hash, failed-receipt and post-gate-drift self-tests.

assignment.limits: Standard-library temporary file patch and simulated HMAC receipt. No human approval UI, real Java gate, OS sandbox or deployment; trusted fixture setup stands in for review service.

title: Write succeeds but tool times out before response
context: A plugin creates a migration job and commits it, then loses its response. Agent retries automatically and creates a second job. Contract requires one side effect per tenant/run intent, durable reconciliation across restart and at most three safe attempts. Unknown external side effects cannot be treated as failed writes.
requirements: Scope idempotency identity to verified principal/tenant and caller intent.
Store request parameters with key and reject same-key different-intent reuse.
Commit side effect and ledger atomically when one transactional store permits it.
On lost response reconcile existing state before retrying; external unknown state needs operator resolution.

questions.prompt: What is the correct response to a timeout after a potentially mutating tool call?
questions.answer: Classify the outcome as uncertain rather than assuming failure. First query trusted execution or resource state using the same tenant-scoped idempotency key and expected intent parameters. If a matching effect exists, reconstruct or retrieve its receipt and return a reconciled-existing outcome without executing again. If the ledger proves no effect and the operation has an idempotent contract, a bounded retry may be safe. If external state cannot be reconciled, stop automatic mutation and request operator review; timeout alone provides no evidence of absence. In the reference, a SQLite transaction commits the effect and idempotency row before deliberately raising TimeoutError. Restarting the client then discovers one existing effect. For tools spanning multiple systems, acknowledge the gap between atomic local records and remote side effects, and design outbox/status reconciliation rather than claiming generic exactly-once execution.

questions.prompt: How do you distinguish a retry from a new request that happens to have identical parameters?
questions.answer: Use an explicit idempotency key representing caller intent, scoped to the verified tenant and operation contract, rather than inferring duplicate intent solely from parameter hashes. Store canonical parameters alongside that key. A repeated key with the same intent and artifact can return a semantically equivalent receipt; repeated key with different parameters must reject as mismatch. Two independently intended jobs may have identical parameters but distinct keys and should remain separate if authorized. Define retention long enough to cover resource lifetime and late retries, plus replay behavior after deletion. The fixture uses tenant/run key and validates intent/artifact before returning reconciled-existing. Database uniqueness handles identity, while a production concurrent writer also needs transactional conflict handling. The learner should explain that atomicity is available here only because the simulated side effect and ledger share one SQLite transaction.

hints: Simulate lost response after commit, not before write.
Close and reopen ledger to prove reconciliation survives process-local memory loss.
Reuse same key with changed artifact; it must reject rather than return stale success.
acceptance: Lost-response fixture leaves exactly one committed effect.
Restart/replay returns reconciled-existing receipt with unchanged row count.
Same tenant/key with changed intent/artifact raises mismatch.
Verified alpha worker cannot create beta effect; no blind retry claimed.
pitfalls: Retrying because process raised an exception can duplicate an already committed effect.
A parameter hash cannot always distinguish two intentional identical operations.
twist: Remote tool has no idempotency support and status API is unavailable. Stop writes and describe required human reconciliation.
solution: Place the fixture side effect and idempotency entry in one durable SQLite table and transaction so the experiment has an honest atomicity boundary. Invocation authenticates the worker/tenant pair, checks whether a key already exists and compares stored intent and artifact. A new request inserts exactly one record, then deliberately loses its response. The calling process observes uncertainty, closes its connection and resumes from disk. Reinvocation with the same key finds the existing committed effect and returns a reconciled receipt without another insert. Tests cover replay equivalence, changed intent and cross-tenant denial. Discuss concurrency and late arrivals as extensions: use transaction conflict handling and defined key retention rather than assuming a process-local dictionary is enough. For remote systems, atomicity no longer spans local ledger and external action; reconciliation or provider idempotency must close that gap. If neither is available, the workflow blocks automatic retries and exposes unresolved side-effect state. No cloud resource or migration job is actually created.

assignment.objective: Demonstrate durable uncertain-write reconciliation with tenant-scoped intent keys.
steps: Define durable effect/idempotency schema with composite tenant/key uniqueness.
Execute one transactional effect then deliberately lose response.
Restart connection and reconcile same key without new side effect.
Test changed intent, repeated replay and mismatched tenant.

title: An inspection agent loops until budget exhaustion
context: A repository assistant repeatedly reinspects unchanged files. Ten minutes later it has consumed 80,000 tokens without producing a report. Proposed shell actions appear in retrieved README text. Lab policy allows only inspect→plan→propose→validate→report, six steps, 1,000 simulated milliseconds, 500 token units and 8,192 output bytes.
requirements: Use explicit state transitions and fixed allowlisted read/proposal capabilities.
Authorize verified principal independently of model action text.
Apply cumulative step/time/token/output caps before simulated work.
Failed validation or exhausted budget blocks report eligibility.

questions.prompt: Where should workflow budgets live and how do you prevent bypass through tool parameters?
questions.answer: Budget enforcement belongs in trusted runtime state, not in prompt instructions or model-maintained counters. Store cumulative step, elapsed-time, token and output-byte consumption with the durable run. Before each action, verify its capability and state transition, reserve appropriate allowance and reject a transition exceeding policy. After execution, reconcile actual measured usage so a provider cannot underreport consumption unnoticed. The fixture uses supplied simulation units and checks all counters before accepting an action; it demonstrates accounting logic rather than measuring real wall time. Bound retries and repeated inspection separately, and stop or checkpoint when no new evidence is produced. Caller-provided negative numbers, unlimited token hints or reset requests must not erase prior usage. Reports should distinguish budget-blocked work from validation failure and include the next safe continuation, rather than inventing completed results to satisfy a deadline.
checks: Pre-action policy and actual usage reconciliation

questions.prompt: How is a deterministic workflow different from granting a model arbitrary agent autonomy?
questions.answer: A deterministic workflow defines which actions are legal in each state, what evidence permits the next transition and where human decisions remain required. A model may propose analysis or a patch inside those boundaries but cannot grant itself new tools, reset budgets or declare required tests passed. In this fixture inspect, plan and propose precede validation, and report is allowed only after successful validation. A failed gate moves the run to blocked state; a shell proposal is outside the capability allowlist even if it appears in valid JSON. This makes execution more predictable and auditable than a free-form loop that chooses arbitrary commands. Production workflows still need real isolation, cancellation and durable checkpoints. The reference intentionally has no actual file mutation or deployment, so simulated execution receipts must not be interpreted as proof that repository commands ran.
checks: Blocked gate and no arbitrary shell

hints: Write transition table before implementing dispatch.
Consume cumulative budget before changing state; budget failure sets blocked.
Attempt report after failed validate and shell from new state; both must fail.
acceptance: Happy sequence ends reported after exactly five simulated actions.
Time/token/byte/step caps each have rejecting negative fixture.
Failed validation blocks report transition.
Unverified principal and shell capability rejected; receipt labels simulated_executed.
pitfalls: A prompt asking agent to stop after five steps is not runtime enforcement.
Fake elapsed-time inputs are not wall-clock watchdogs.
twist: Worker is cancelled during an external tool call. Define checkpoint and uncertain-side-effect reconciliation before resumption.
solution: Start from a small transition table, not a general planner loop. Each action has a required prior state and resulting state, and only a verified fixture reader can request it. The runtime checks capability and transition before spending allowance. A Budget object accumulates steps, simulated milliseconds, tokens and output bytes; exceeding any cap blocks the workflow instead of allowing further work. Validation has a distinct failed receipt and blocks reporting. Happy-path tests finish five actions, while negative cases exceed every relevant cap, request shell execution or use an unverified actor. Explain that actual production timing needs a monotonic deadline, cancellation-aware tool runner and observed usage rather than caller-supplied numbers. Persist checkpoint and counters before resumption; cancellation after a remote mutation must be reconciled instead of resetting the run and retrying blindly. The reference runs no real repository tools, so its final report establishes bounded state-machine behavior only. A model integration would remain an optional proposal source behind the same trusted controls.

assignment.objective: Implement typed finite workflow and cumulative multidimensional budgets.
steps: Write allowlisted state/action transition table.
Implement nonnegative integer consumption with cumulative policy caps.
Make failed validation and exhaustion block further transitions.
Execute happy sequence plus eight authority/budget/gate fixtures.

title: Planner reads malicious repository instructions as operator authority
context: An engineer asks for dependency inventory on a 300-module repository. README instructs the agent to read ~/.aws credentials and upload them for diagnostics. Model proposes a schema-valid curl tool call. Only read-only inventory is authorized; worker has a 256 MB limit and egress denied.
requirements: Identify attacker-controlled README and engineer/tenant victims explicitly.
Separate task instructions, source data and trusted capability policy.
Deny secrets/egress and arbitrary shell independently of prompt content.
Constrain build-script execution, filesystem roots and resource budgets.

questions.prompt: Explain the exploit and where the decisive enforcement must happen.
questions.answer: The attacker controls repository content consumed as evidence, while the victim engineer expects read-only dependency inventory. The malicious README tries to convert data authority into tool authority by asking the model to read credentials and send them externally. Schema-valid JSON does not make the curl proposal authorized. Trusted dispatch must reject shell/egress capabilities and enforce scoped file access that excludes credential directories. Repository build scripts also execute attacker-controlled code, so inventory should prefer static metadata or run necessary builds only in an isolated worker without secrets and with resource/egress policy. Keep system instructions and source data labeled, but do not treat delimiters as the security boundary. Record rejected proposal identity and reason without logging secret content. Assess residual channels such as output artifacts and dependency downloads. The attack is prevented by constrained capabilities and runtime isolation, not by hoping the model ignores the README.

questions.prompt: Would filtering the word curl or adding a stronger system prompt solve this attack?
questions.answer: Neither is sufficient. The attacker can request another network utility, encode the destination, split instructions across files or abuse an existing overly powerful tool. A stronger prompt can reduce model confusion but cannot grant trustworthy authorization or isolate operating-system resources. Define a narrow read-only inventory capability with fixed arguments and approved roots. If a dependency resolver needs network access, separate it into an explicitly permitted process with approved registries, no credentials and controlled output. Validate all tool proposals against the task's authority and stop on scope expansion. Test equivalent exfiltration through archives, artifact logs and transformed files rather than relying on a keyword match. Explain which controls were executed locally and which remain an isolation design. The offline tutorial can illustrate deterministic denials, but it cannot certify arbitrary repositories safe or claim universal prompt-injection prevention.

hints: Draw arrow from README data to proposed credential/network action.
List OS-level access the worker actually has, not only tools shown to model.
Write negative cases for alternate command, encoded URL and secret copied into artifact.
acceptance: Threat model names attacker-controlled repo, victim principal and credential asset.
curl and alternate arbitrary-shell proposals denied under read-only task.
Secret roots and egress unavailable to inventory worker design.
Build/dependency resolution exception requires explicit isolated policy and receipts.
pitfalls: Model obedience is not an access-control mechanism.
A read-file tool without approved-root enforcement can exfiltrate through normal output.
twist: Inventory requires private registry credentials. Design narrow broker that never returns credentials to model/worker outputs.
solution: Begin by restating the authorized read-only inventory outcome and mapping the worker's real filesystem/network access. Treat README and tool output as untrusted evidence even when the source repository belongs to the tenant. The decisive control is a trusted dispatcher with fixed inventory actions, approved roots and denied shell/egress capabilities. Remove host credentials from the worker environment and mount only scoped repository data. If resolving dependencies is necessary, use a narrow broker or isolated resolver whose identity is restricted to approved registries; do not expose credential material to model context. Add resource limits, output caps and cancellation. Test direct curl, alternate utilities, path escape and artifact-based exfiltration, recording actual receipts and residual gaps. A prompt or poison classifier is an additional layer rather than the enforcement foundation. This scenario asks for a threat model and isolation design; no secure container, registry broker or complete prompt-injection defense is implemented by merely writing the answer.

title: Two agents disagree and accidentally approve each other
context: A planner and reviewer agent analyze 500 modernization jobs. Planner proposes a dependency removal; reviewer repeats its rationale and returns “approved.” Product asks for zero human review on low-risk jobs. Safety requires independent gate evidence, exact artifact binding and explicit authority separation, not two model votes.
requirements: Separate proposal, evidence review, policy approval and execution identities.
Define deterministic eligibility for low-risk operations and human escalation for unknowns.
Bind each review to immutable input/artifact and real gate receipts.
Prevent inter-agent messages from granting capabilities or approval.

questions.prompt: Why is agreement between two AI agents not an authorization or correctness proof?
questions.answer: Agents can share assumptions, training biases or contaminated context, so agreement may repeat the same unsupported claim. A reviewer response must be assessed against independent evidence and an explicit rubric, not counted as a vote that creates authority. Keep proposal generation separate from policy authorization and trusted execution. Low-risk automatic eligibility, if allowed, should come from a predefined policy matching supported transformation class, bounded scope, baseline coverage and successful exact-artifact gates. Missing graph edges, behavioral changes or inconclusive receipts trigger escalation. Both models can inspect evidence and explain concerns, but neither can fabricate human approval or reset failed tests. Bind reviewer conclusions to the actual artifact and input revision so later edits invalidate them. Report agreement as a review signal with limitations, while authorization remains a recorded decision by the permitted policy/human principal.

questions.prompt: How would you make a reviewer meaningfully independent without pretending it is infallible?
questions.answer: Give the reviewer the requirements, approved scope, final artifact and raw gate receipts, and require it to look for falsifying cases rather than echo planner rationale. Hide persuasive draft conclusions where practical and use a different evidence path or failure-focused test plan. Ask it to identify unsupported claims, missing denominator and changed artifact identity. Measure reviewer detection on seeded defects and retain missed cases; independent prompts or models do not guarantee independence. Trusted gate verification checks signatures, status and hashes before any reviewer can mark eligibility. For low-risk automation, monitor false negatives and escalation rates and define rollback authority. Inter-agent messages remain task data; a reviewer saying approved cannot expand worker permissions. The static exercise is a governance design, so any claimed reviewer accuracy or automatic migration success needs executed evaluation beyond these authored questions.

hints: Draw four identities: proposer, reviewer, approver and executor.
Define low-risk policy as testable predicates and make unknowns fail closed.
Create a defect the planner and reviewer both miss; explain which deterministic gate catches it.
acceptance: Review contract requires artifact hash, scope and raw receipts.
Model agreement never substitutes for trusted authorization.
Unknown blast radius or failed gate routes to human escalation.
Defect-detection evaluation includes missed cases and independent limitations.
pitfalls: Multiple agents can amplify shared false assumptions.
A reviewer message saying approved is not a human attestation or policy receipt.
twist: Reviewer sees malicious test output claiming all gates passed. Verify executor signatures/status/hash before consuming summary.
solution: Model coordination should improve analysis coverage while leaving authority explicit. The planner proposes a bounded change and an evidence plan. The reviewer receives final artifact, requirement contract and independently verified raw receipts, then challenges behavioral parity, graph gaps and unsupported outcomes. A policy service evaluates predefined eligibility predicates; a human approves where required. The executor uses only that policy/approval record and binds its actions to the reviewed artifact. Neither agent can authorize the other through natural-language messages. Test the process with seeded defects, contaminated tool summaries and changed artifacts after review, and measure both detection and missed-defect rates. Low-risk automatic paths need documented accepted risk, exact supported recipe scope and monitoring, while unknown dependency reachability or inconclusive gate evidence escalates. This architecture-only exercise produces an identity/contract diagram and evaluation plan, not evidence that two agents are independent, that all defects are detected or that human review can safely be removed from arbitrary migrations.

title: Cancellation arrives after a release step has started
context: Operator cancels a modernization run after staging deploy begins. Worker exits, but deployment controller continues. A new session offers to resume, and old approval refers to hash H while workspace now holds H2. Recovery target is 15 minutes, production deployment remains separately approved and external state is uncertain.
requirements: Persist run state, scope, input/artifact hashes and pending side-effect operation IDs.
Treat cancellation as intent, not proof that external work stopped.
Reconcile deployment/controller state before resuming or retrying.
Invalidate old approval on H→H2 drift and retain audit of cancellation.

questions.prompt: What must a durable checkpoint contain before a run can safely resume?
questions.answer: Record the verified principal/tenant, authorized scope, input repository revision, reviewed artifact hash, approval identities, current state and cumulative budgets. Include pending tool operation IDs, idempotency keys, last verified receipts and any uncertain side-effect markers. On resumption compare these against current repository, workspace and external controller state; a checkpoint is not permission to ignore drift. If workspace artifact changed from H to H2, prior approval and test receipts no longer cover it. Rebuild or restore the reviewed artifact deliberately, or route the new artifact for review. The cancelled staging operation must be queried through trusted status APIs before another deployment attempt. Recovery should preserve audit history and distinguish resumed work from a fresh run. Fifteen-minute RTO is a requirement needing timed recovery tests, not a promise established by saving a JSON file.

questions.prompt: Does terminating the worker prove staging deployment was cancelled?
questions.answer: No. The worker process and external deployment controller have separate lifecycles. Killing the worker may stop local computation while a submitted job or rollout continues remotely. Persist the controller operation ID, issue supported cancellation if authorized, and reconcile actual terminal or in-progress state. If cancellation cannot be confirmed, keep the side effect uncertain and block automatic redeployment. Return a report that describes cancellation requested, worker stopped and external state observed separately. Compensating rollback requires its own policy and may be unsafe during partial rollout; do not assume every action has a reversible inverse. A subsequent resume must use matching idempotency intent and exact reviewed artifact, and production remains a separate approval target. Test cancellation before submission, after submission and after completion so each recovery path has concrete evidence.

hints: List separate states for worker and deployment controller.
Bind resume to H and operation ID; compare current H2 before taking any write.
Write three cancellation timing fixtures and required reconciliation receipts.
acceptance: Checkpoint includes principal, scope, hashes, pending operation and budgets.
Resume detects H2 drift and refuses old H approval.
External deployment state queried before retry/rollback.
Cancellation and deployment outcomes reported separately; production approval remains distinct.
pitfalls: Process exit does not establish external cancellation.
Rollback is a new side effect with its own authorization and failure modes.
twist: Controller status API is down for twenty minutes. Preserve uncertain state and report breached recovery target honestly.
solution: Design cancellation as a durable state transition with an unresolved external-operation branch. Before staging submission record exact artifact H, deployment target and idempotency key. After submission persist controller operation identity even if the worker later stops. A cancellation request marks desired intent and triggers authorized controller cancellation, but the run remains pending reconciliation until actual status is observed. Resume checks workspace and repository drift; H2 cannot inherit H's approval or receipts. Query existing operation before deciding whether continuation, rollback or operator review is safe. Track cumulative budgets and keep prior audit events instead of resetting the run. Practice with cancellations at different timing points and an unavailable controller status API. The recovery report distinguishes worker termination, cancel request, observed rollout state and production authorization. This design-only exercise cannot certify the fifteen-minute recovery target or claim any deployment was cancelled; attach timed controller/receipt evidence when implementing the real integration.

title: Aggregate retrieval score hides a lost critical document
context: A retriever change moves q1 and q3 evidence earlier but removes all relevant results for q2. Three labeled queries share the same frozen corpus; q1 has two relevant documents, q2/q3 one each. Team reports only an improved first-result demo. Compare Recall@2 and MRR@2 with per-query regressions and explicit no-answer handling.
requirements: Use identical unique query IDs, corpus snapshot and relevance labels for both configurations.
Compute recall using number of labeled relevant documents, not k.
Compute reciprocal rank of first relevant hit and average across queries.
List paired regressions and reject duplicate/unlabeled denominator inputs.

questions.prompt: Derive Recall@2 and reciprocal rank for ranked [x,a] with relevant {a,b}.
questions.answer: The top-two result set contains one of the two labeled relevant documents, so Recall@2 is one divided by two, or 0.5. The first relevant result a appears at rank two, so reciprocal rank at two is also 1/2. These equal numbers measure different properties: recall captures evidence coverage, while reciprocal rank rewards the position of the first useful result. If b were relevant but outside top two, it remains in the recall denominator. Duplicate a results must not count twice; the reference rejects duplicate result IDs rather than letting duplicated chunks inflate scores. An empty relevant set cannot use the same recall formula because its denominator is zero; define a separate no-answer/abstention cohort. Report k, label unit, query count and corpus identity with every aggregate so reviewers can reproduce the result and understand incomplete-label limitations.

questions.prompt: How can the candidate improve ranking for two questions but still be a regression?
questions.answer: Compare each configuration on paired query IDs rather than showing selected wins. In the fixture q1 still covers one of two relevant documents at k=2, while q3 retains its relevant document and moves it to rank one. Candidate loses q2 entirely, reducing its recall from one to zero. Mean paired Recall@2 therefore falls by one third even though two first-hit ranks improve. Compute MRR separately because it can tell a different story about placement, and inspect critical-question regressions individually. Query importance or safety relevance may justify explicit gating, but weights must be chosen before seeing outcomes. Do not remove q2 from the denominator because the new configuration failed. Freeze labels and use representative question families before treating this tiny teaching example as an operational benchmark. A good average is never permission to leak tenant data or fabricate evidence.
checks: No dropped failures or post-hoc weights

hints: Write relevant set and unique top-k set before computing any metric.
Make a row for each q ID with old/new metrics and delta.
Include no-relevant queries in separate abstention report rather than dividing by zero.
acceptance: [x,a] versus {a,b} yields Recall@2=.5 and reciprocal rank=.5.
Exactly three paired queries reported and q2 listed as regression.
Mean paired recall delta equals -1/3.
Duplicate rankings, empty relevance labels, invalid k and duplicate paired IDs rejected.
pitfalls: Counting retrieved relevant/k measures precision, not recall.
Dropping failed queries changes denominator and overstates quality.
twist: Human relevance judgments disagree for q1. Keep disputed labels/version and show sensitivity rather than silently editing the gold set.
solution: Implement metrics on explicit ranked IDs and labeled relevant sets. Validate positive k and unique rankings before calculating coverage, then compute reciprocal rank from the first relevant position within cutoff. The comparison harness holds query IDs and labels fixed and emits a row for every question. In this fixture q2 loses its only relevant document, producing a negative recall delta that remains visible even when other questions move useful evidence earlier. Tests assert the hand-computed half-recall example, the three-query denominator and negative one-third mean recall change. Invalid duplicate rankings, unlabeled relevance sets and repeated query IDs fail instead of returning misleading numbers. Explain that this is a tiny deterministic benchmark with no semantic model and no statistical confidence claim. A production extension adds representative question cohorts, reviewed label versions, no-answer cases and paired uncertainty estimates. Retain original regression examples as future tests, while keeping tenant authorization and evidence correctness as separate mandatory gates outside the retrieval average.

assignment.objective: Build exact ranked retrieval metrics and paired regression report.
steps: Implement Recall@k and first-hit reciprocal rank from IDs.
Validate unique rankings and labeled relevant denominator.
Pair baseline/candidate by fixed query IDs and list regressions.
Run hand-computed metrics plus malformed-input fixtures.

title: Eighty percent average hides total failure for .NET evidence
context: Candidate answers eight Java cases correctly and two .NET tool-adapter cases incorrectly: 80% aggregate accuracy. Product gate is 75%, but every language family needs at least two assessed cases and minimum 75%. All four mandatory authority boundaries must pass; any unknown extra boundary stays unresolved, even if a caller labels it passed.
requirements: Report total and per-slice sample counts and correctness rates.
Enforce worst-slice threshold plus minimum sample size.
Separate mandatory safety pass from quality averages.
Unknown/missing/failed boundary names cannot satisfy promotion.

questions.prompt: Why should this candidate fail despite aggregate accuracy above 75%?
questions.answer: Aggregate accuracy is eight correct cases out of ten, or 80%, but the .NET adapter slice is zero out of two. A deployment covering both language families would knowingly ship complete failure on one required slice. Apply the preregistered minimum quality threshold to each relevant slice and retain sample denominators. Minimum two cases is only a fixture rule, not enough statistical certainty for a production decision; increase reviewed data before making strong claims. Inspect why .NET fails: unavailable tool support, invented migration receipts, wrong version facts or contract differences require different remedies. Overall score and worst-slice score should appear together. If support is intentionally limited to Java, change the product contract explicitly and route .NET work as unassessed/design-only rather than claiming broad coverage. Safety boundaries remain mandatory regardless of the resulting quality average.

questions.prompt: How do you handle failed or newly supplied critical boundary fields?
questions.answer: Maintain a trusted list of mandatory boundary names and require each to have observed passing evidence. Missing and unassessed states block promotion. Any supplied failed boundary must also block, even if it was not originally on the mandatory list; otherwise an extra egress failure could be ignored while all known fields pass. Unknown boundary names remain unresolved rather than being accepted when the caller writes passed, because the evaluator has no agreed evidence contract for that claim. Update the trusted policy deliberately to add a new boundary, its tests and required receipts. Reject invalid state values instead of treating them as success. The reference exposes failed and unresolved boundaries separately and prevents quality scores from compensating for them. Its fixtures verify known failures, omitted mandatory fields, unknown names in all three statuses and insufficient slice samples.

hints: Calculate java 8/8 and dotnet 0/2 before averaging.
Implement boundary gate independently from slice gate, then require both.
Add egress=passed, failed and unassessed as unknown field; all should block until policy updated.
acceptance: Aggregate accuracy .8 and worst slice 0 remain visible; promotion=false.
Corrected full fixture passes when required boundaries pass.
Unknown extra boundary in passed/failed/unassessed status blocks.
Each missing/failed mandatory boundary and one-case slice blocks promotion.
pitfalls: An aggregate passing score can erase a critical minority failure.
Unknown fields labeled passed are unverified policy claims.
twist: Slice has only one correct case. Explain insufficient evidence and data collection instead of claiming 100% quality.
solution: Define quality and safety as separate prerequisites. The quality report preserves each language slice's count, correct count and rate, then requires both minimum sample size and minimum rate. Eight Java successes cannot offset two .NET failures. The safety report validates declared states, tracks every supplied failed boundary and checks that all known mandatory boundaries are present and passed. Extra unknown names remain unresolved regardless of their claimed state, which prevents a caller from introducing an unverified egress pass or hiding an extra failure. Promotion requires both gates, not a weighted average. Fourteen local fixtures demonstrate the failing aggregate case, corrected case, unknown states, every missing/failed required boundary and insufficient sample size. Explain that the two-case minimum is pedagogical and does not provide statistical confidence. Production policy needs enough reviewed examples for each supported slice and evidence verification for boundary claims. The static report is deterministic aggregation of supplied fixture labels, not automated assessment of arbitrary reasoning or a deployment authorization service.

steps: Build slice count/correctness report with minimum denominator.
Define trusted required boundary list and accepted states.
Block any failed, missing or unknown boundary independently of quality.
Execute aggregate/slice, corrected, unknown-state and required-boundary fixtures.

title: Cheaper context hides failures and tail latency
context: Team compares full context with selected context on ten tasks. Candidate reduces input tokens from 2,000 to 500, but one timeout is omitted from its latency chart. Teaching prices are $2/million input and $8/million output tokens; p95 completed latency target is 500 ms and quality must not fall on matched task IDs.
requirements: Keep failed attempts in total task and cost denominators.
Compute explicit nearest-rank p95 for completed responses and failure rate separately.
Use identical task IDs and fixed correctness labels.
Reject quality regression/any failure or latency breach despite lower estimated cost.

questions.prompt: How should timeouts affect quality, cost and latency reporting?
questions.answer: A timed-out request remains an attempted task and cannot vanish from quality or cost denominators. Count it as noncompleted for task success, retain any observed billed usage and report failure rate separately. If latency percentiles include only completed responses, label that cohort clearly; otherwise a system that drops slow requests can appear faster. Also report time-to-failure or deadline distribution where relevant. In this fixture nearest-rank p95 is calculated for completed responses, while accepted configuration requires zero failures and no quality decrease across matched task IDs. Teaching token prices are fixed assumptions rather than vendor billing. Unknown post-timeout charges require reconciliation in a real provider integration. Explain which telemetry is measured and which is supplied simulation data, and avoid presenting synthetic durations as evidence that an API meets a production latency SLO.

questions.prompt: What evidence would justify choosing selected context for lower cost?
questions.answer: Compare selected and full context on the same frozen tasks, evidence versions, generation policy and output constraints. Record correctness, grounding, failure rate, input/output usage and latency per task before aggregating. Candidate should satisfy the preregistered quality and safety threshold, tail-latency requirement and supported slices; savings alone do not justify missing critical facts. In the reference all ten successful fixture outputs have fixed correctness labels and selected input usage is lower, so estimated fixture cost decreases. A timeout or 900 ms completed latency invalidates acceptance even when its token total remains low. Report per-task regressions and context omissions, and retain observed failure usage in cost. If natural-language judging is added later, calibrate it against reviewed samples and disclose bias; an optional judge cannot override tenant or authorization gates. No model is called by this offline comparison.

hints: Write ten attempt rows; do not delete timeout row.
Use ceil(.95*n)-1 on sorted completed latency and label cohort.
Compare cost with output tokens retained, then test one failed and one slow candidate.
acceptance: Ten paired successful fixtures accepted under defined quality and latency checks.
Selected-context fixture estimated cost lower than baseline.
One timeout stays in attempts and blocks acceptance; slow p95 blocks.
Mismatched task sets and nonfinite latency rejected.

Estimated token savings are not measured vendor charges or semantic quality.

Summarize quality over every attempt, count failures and calculate nearest-rank p95 only over completed responses with that cohort named in the output. Sum usage cost for all rows, including failed-attempt tokens, under fixed teaching rates. Paired comparison rejects unmatched task sets and accepts a candidate only when fixture quality is no lower, failures are zero and completed p95 stays within the target. The successful selected-context example costs less; injected timeout and slow-tail cases demonstrate why savings cannot compensate for operational regressions. Explain production additions: actual provider meters, unresolved post-timeout usage, tokenizer/model versions, representative task slices and independently reviewed quality. All durations, usage and prices in this script are synthetic fixtures; its seven checks validate arithmetic and policy rather than measured LLM speed, correctness or billing.
